records.name: Santa Catarina
records.summary: Direction: worse than national — the only Brazilian state to have enacted a statutory bathroom restriction, and the venue of a nationally decisive refusal. Lei 19.686 of 21 January 2026 requires every educational institution in the state — basic, fundamental, secondary, technical and higher — to provide bathrooms separately by sex, banning shared or unisex installation and use, with fines of up to R$10,000; a second bill approved 22 December 2025 extends the ban to state and municipal public administration bodies; a third, tabled October 2025, would restrict school and locker-room use to the sex recorded on the birth certificate — continued legislative escalation rather than a one-off. The nationally decisive case arose here: a trans woman was refused entry to the women's bathroom by staff at a Florianópolis shopping centre, urinated on herself in front of shoppers and had to take public transport home; on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Tribunal rejected her appeal, leaving refusals lawful under ordinary private-premises rules. In the other direction, Florianópolis has a visible LGBTQ tourism scene with pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages and marker changes; nationwide legal rights are identical, so visitors see the same federal protections as elsewhere. Caveat: state violence statistics sit atop the country's nationally leading lethality and should be read partly as reporting density rather than as gender-specific exposure.

records.name: British Columbia
records.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): BC: consistently Canada's most progressive province on LGBT issues (first human-rights code inclusion 1992); Vancouver Davie Village scene. Regional evidence: no hostile provincial legislation, but a documented 2023 wave of coordinated disruptions against public drag-storytime events at libraries — Coquitlam Public Library postponed/cancelled repeatedly (Jan 14 2023 protest at the Town Centre branch; Oct 13 2023 postponement) under "public safety risk" claims, with a counter-gathering becoming the largest queer gathering the Tri-Cities had seen; at a Richmond library event with no police on scene a man pushed through to photograph the performer; a Granville Island children's drag camp was threatened and required a public rally of support. Scored relative to the national score (0.86) for Canada.

records.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Valparaíso/Viña: Chile's bohemian port-university culture; criminality is general rather than gender-targeted. Regional evidence: by a wide margin the country's highest-incidence region for anti-LGBTI discrimination - in 2024 it concentrated 51.32% of all national recorded cases (Metropolitana second at 25.12%), up 80.93% over 2023. In 2025 recorded cases fell here alongside Metropolitana while all 14 other regions rose; Movilh reads this as a decentralisation of hate toward territories with less LGBTIQ visibility and debate, not a local improvement. Scored relative to the national score (0.72) for Chile.

records.name: Antioquia
records.summary:
Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent record on anti-trans killings. On 4 April 2025 in Bello, a 32-year-old trans woman, Sara Millerey González Borja, was beaten and thrown into a waterway while onlookers filmed her; she died of her injuries. She was the third LGBT person killed in Bello that year — the first two were gay men — and the case triggered vigils, protests in several cities and a presidential order to investigate, amid a national tally of 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

The national frame around that series, as documented: more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023 (41 recorded) and eight more between February and April 2024; armed groups in at least one southern department have circulated flyers announcing 'social cleansing' against trans women, in territories where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement. The surviving record supports a lethal concentration around Antioquia's metro area — three municipal killings within four months — and documents no province-level protection machinery specific to it.

records.name: Bogota Capital District
records.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Bogotá Capital District: the best-documented trans community and services in the country, alongside a documented police-violence pattern in its tolerance zone. Regional evidence: Red Comunitaria Trans reported police shouting at, baton-beating and shooting at trans sex workers at 3:50 a.m. on a central street (the district mayor's office took up the case); two trans women were killed within hours of each other on the night of 2 January 2026 (a 24-year-old in Engativá, a 20-year-old in Florida Blanca); a 32-year-old trans activist was found dead in the eastern hills in December 2023, with the press itself framing 'the recurring mechanisms in crimes against trans women'. The district's own law journal published a study of violence against trans people in the Santa Fe tolerance zone, where sector expulsions push people into other localities. Mass identity-check operations: 200+ officers in San Bernardo (April 2025) and over 1,200 uniformed officers with background and migrant control in Santa Fe (January 2026) - a visibly gender-nonconforming person in central Bogotá is therefore statistically likely to be in the path of a sweep. Scored relative to the national score (0.52) for Colombia.

records.name: Comunidad de Madrid
records.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Madrid (Chueca): among the most visible LGBT urban scenes in Europe; total anonymity in daily life; Pride among the continent's largest. Regional evidence: the one community that has used its own legislative power to narrow trans law - Ley 17/2023 and Ley 18/2023 (both 27 December 2023) amended the community's own 2016 gender-identity law and its anti-LGBTBI law on the stated ground of protecting freedom of expression and academic freedom, stripping the provisions that obliged educational institutions; Ley 1/2022 centres parents as primary responsible parties and structures school opt-outs (the 'pin parental' mechanism in Madrid schools). Evidentiary caveat: Madrid's citizens report LGTBI hate-crime offences to reporting services more than any other community's, so low recorded hostility here is not available as an alibi - the divergence is statutory, not statistical. Scored relative to the national score (0.88) for Spain.

records.name: Bourgogne-Franche-Comté
records.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Dijon / Cote-d'Or: rural traditional department. Regional evidence: the only prefecture in the country found to have twice banned a Pride march from its city centre with the ban upheld - on 12 June 2025 the prefecture prohibited the Pride 2025 march in central Dijon citing "risk of trouble to public order", the second consecutive year of the same restriction; the organisers' withdrawal citing LGBT visibility was itself called significant by the city. On 14 June 2025 the administrative court rejected the legal challenge, and the march (about 1,500 people per police) proceeded on a diverted route around the historic centre; the prefecture justified the ban by estimated organiser numbers (200 vs previous 2,500 and 1,500 turnouts) and a stated risk of violent individuals attaching themselves. The march itself passed peacefully ("joyful and festive, without a hitch") - the harm documented here is the restriction and its chilling effect, not violence. Scored relative to the national score (0.67) for France.

records.name: Hauts-de-France
records.summary:
The region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk is prison placement, which national law sets: under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a trans prisoner is held according to the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still marked male are placed in all-male facilities. An investigation published in January 2018 recorded exactly that near the region's principal city: Paola, shouted at and threatened by inmates during three days in a men's facility after a 2014 transfer, and — in the capital — Kara B., held under notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial; the national detention inspector-general calls transgender detainees the group that suffers most in custody.

The inspector-general's May 2021 opinion, covering every place of deprivation of liberty in the state and built from some forty referrals since 2010, finds serious violations persisting: isolation by reason of trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never translated into prison rules. It recommends that detainees choose the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation and trans-only wings, and requires continuity of hormone and medical care — recommendations whose non-implementation is itself part of the documented picture for visitors who are detained anywhere in the state, including here.
